title: Jeremiah 49:23–27
context: The LORD of Armies speaks through Jeremiah concerning Damascus, the leading city of Aram (Syria). Hamath and Arpad, commonly identified as cities to the north of Damascus, are shaken by bad news; Damascus itself grows feeble, turns to flee, and is seized with anguish. The LORD asks how the city of praise, the city of joy, has not been forsaken, a line interpreters read in different ways, and says its young men and soldiers will fall silent. He will kindle a fire in its wall that will devour the palaces of Ben Hadad, a royal name borne by several kings of Damascus (compare 1 Kings 20:1). The final line closely resembles Amos 1:4, and the oracle can be read alongside Isaiah 17:1. The text does not specify when or by whom the judgment comes. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage as shared ground about God’s sovereignty over every city and the passing of human glory.

verses.text: Of Damascus: “Hamath and Arpad are confounded, for they have heard evil news. They have melted away. There is sorrow on the sea. It can’t be quiet.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hamath and Arpad confounded by bad news and melting away. Fear spreads among the cities of the region.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the anxiety of nations who hear of coming judgment. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the identifications of Hamath and Arpad with appropriate care (compare Isaiah 36:19).

verses.text: Damascus has grown feeble, she turns herself to flee, and trembling has seized her. Anguish and sorrows have taken hold of her, as of a woman in travail.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Damascus grown feeble, turning to flee, and seized with anguish like a woman in labor. Strength gives way to fear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the proud city humbled before God. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober picture of collapse.

verses.text: How is the city of praise not forsaken, the city of my joy?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking how the city of praise and joy has not been forsaken. Its former glory makes its fall more striking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a lament over a famous city. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the precise sense of the line with care, while seeing the passing of human glory.

verses.text: Therefore her young men will fall in her streets, and all the men of war will be brought to silence in that day,” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD of Armies saying the young men and soldiers will fall silent in that day. Military strength offers no protection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s judgment reaching the city’s defenders. Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, without dwelling on its details.

verses.text: “I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it will devour the palaces of Ben Hadad.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD kindling a fire in the wall of Damascus that will devour the palaces of Ben Hadad. Royal power will not endure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the close parallel with Amos 1:4. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober statement of God’s rule over kings.
